extracted.intended_audience: instructors/teachers of undergraduate discrete mathematics and proof-based mathematics courses
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and running an undergraduate discrete mathematics course using the Bogart guided group discovery method (adapting notes, structuring problems, class logistics, grading, and teaching proof/logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols in notes to assist students and instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbols assist the student and they also provide important cues for an instructor who wants to design a cohesive set of mandatory problems to be completed by the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear symbolic cues in notes so students get guidance and instructors can select/sequence mandatory problems coherently; symbols should support both student learning and instructor planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning strategy: group discovery / cooperative learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The learning strategy of group discovery is based on the premise that most students learn well from working cooperatively with peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure class time to have students actively involved in their own learning during class and outside; prioritize group work over pure expository lecture where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment balance between group work and individual accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike many classes in which an expository lecture is the primary medium for conveying information, students in group discovery classes are actively involved in their own learning during class as well as outside the classroom. In the Bogart implementation of group discovery, most of the course grade comes from non-group work, including traditional in-class exams and the expectation that final solutions will be completed without consultation or collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure majority of grading assesses individual understanding (exams, final independent write-ups) while allowing group activity for learning; require final written solutions to be done independently to preserve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor balance: give time vs ensure progress
rubrics_metrics.description: During class time, the instructor must work to achieve a balance between giving students sufficient time to work successfully in groups and ensuring students are satisfactorily progressing through the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor groups, guide some to push ahead or stay on core problems; adjust pacing to keep most students roughly aligned through chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor guidance via selective large-group discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor also guides by providing selective and thoughtful use of discussion which involves the whole class or a large portion of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whole-class discussion to review, to model successful group dynamics without an all-knowing participant, and to rescue groups that think they've hit dead ends; time and frequency of such discussion may vary by instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling successful group dynamics in large-group discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: An interesting use of large-group discussion is to model successful group dynamics with no all-knowing participant. This can be especially effective when it is used at times when most of the students think they have hit a dead end on a problem sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstrations of group problem-solving and patient listening to show how groups make progress; encourage public explanation of partial attempts and difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fostering student responsibility and initiation of discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Guided discovery would strengthen the students’ sense of their own responsibility for their learning, and the instructor would foster an atmosphere where students themselves initiate discussions which involve a large percentage of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to initiate and lead discussions; set expectations that students take responsibility for learning and for bringing group questions to the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt notes: expand basic material into early chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ken’s original notes assumed a familiarity with basic topics ... that we cannot expect from our students when they enter this course. In the adaptation, this basic material has been expanded and incorporated into the fabric of the early chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate prerequisite review material into early chapters rather than relegating it to appendices to reduce flipping and to help students see connections; keep a few short appendices for scanning only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move advanced material to optional sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the topic of Ken’s course was enumerative combinatorics, some of his problem sequences cover material that is not basic to our more general syllabus of discrete mathematics. In our adaptation, much of that advanced material has been moved to optional sections which are not required in the mainstream problem sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide optional/problematic advanced sequences for motivated students to pursue without burdening the mainstream syllabus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chunk large chapters to encourage frequent review
rubrics_metrics.description: Ken’s first chapter was very long, and we have spread that material over three chapters in the adaptation. The new presentation encourages students to review frequently and tries to facilitate that summarizing process by packaging the material in more obvious units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break long chapters into smaller units, provide summarizing handouts per chapter to aid review and instructor tailoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add formal definitions, theorem statements, and example proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since many of our students don’t have sufficient mathematical maturity to ferret out the definitions and theorems from the exercises, we have added more formal definitions, more statements of theorems, and an occasional example of a complete mathematical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make key definitions and theorems explicit in the text and give occasional worked proofs to scaffold students who lack experience with extracting formal statements from exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify expected level of solution (complete proof vs informal explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some problems had to be re-worded to distinguish between whether a complete proof is expected or whether a less-formal explanation would suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly indicate for each problem whether a full formal proof is required or a less formal justification is acceptable; use wording to set clear expectations for proof rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize conceptual development of function (object stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem solver’s understanding of function must have evolved from plugging values into a given function through determining whether or not a relation is a function. In fact, he or she should recognize how the notion of function is useful for the problem and then construct the proper function; that is, the student must have at least arrived at the object stage of conceptualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design problem sequences and exercises that move students from procedural use of functions to recognizing and constructing functions as mathematical objects; include tasks that require determining whether a relation is a function and building bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize equivalence relations and quotient principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The adaptation’s emphasis on equivalence relations ... using equivalence relations is an important skill to be obtained from a beginning course in discrete mathematics and is expected in later courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a full chapter on equivalence relations, rework quotient-principle problems into equivalence relation frameworks, and expand sequences to show broader applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce mathematical induction earlier and with varied problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction now occurs earlier in the adaptation, and more problems have been added, including a new sequence which builds student understanding of inductive processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach induction early, present varied induction problems (beyond formulaic exercises) that require identifying underlying inductive processes and relate induction to other proof techniques such as smallest-counterexample arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course logistics: meeting frequency, session length, and immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: The classes now meet twice a week in 75-minute sessions in order to provide sufficient immersion in the problems. For the first few years the classes met in 100-minute blocks, but we found it was more difficult for everyone to remain on task for that amount of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer two shorter meetings per week (e.g., 75 minutes) rather than a single long block to maintain engagement and productivity in group problem work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment rhythm and group composition
rubrics_metrics.description: With our classes meeting on Mondays and Wednesdays, the usual format has been to assign a range of problem numbers on Monday, and this forms a minimal assignment to be completed by the beginning of the following Monday’s class. Students spend class time working in four-person groups that have usually been formed by the instructor and whose composition changes about every other week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a weekly assignment schedule, use small instructor-formed groups (e.g., four-person), rotate group membership periodically to expose students to diverse peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem completion expectations and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ken required students to solve 90% of the problems by the end of the term. ... It has been reasonable to expect the students to work about twenty problems a week for the first few weeks ... as the term proceeds ... completing about 12–15 problems is a reasonable expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic weekly target numbers that decrease as difficulty increases; aim for high overall completion (e.g., 90%) while adjusting mandatory lists as term progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick and frequent feedback with structured resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: We have all found that quick and frequent feedback is essential, and our goal has been to collect written work on Monday and to return the graded work two days later in Wednesday’s class. Ken’s method allows for unlimited re-submission of problems, but in our classes both the number of re-submissions and the re-submittal window are restricted and varies according to the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect work frequently and return graded work rapidly (e.g., within 48 hours); allow limited resubmissions within a specified window and cap number of resubmissions per student to manage workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading scale and modifications (0—5—9/10 triage, adding 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: All instructors have used our modification of Ken’s 0—5—9/10 'triage' grading-scale, adding a possible grade of 7 as a compensation for fewer resubmits. Some instructors have assigned a separate grade which specifically assesses student writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a triage-style grading scale to indicate levels of completeness; consider intermediate scores (e.g., 7) to reward near-complete work when resubmits are limited; optionally assess mathematical writing separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which problems to grade: variety of approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Some instructors collect all assigned problems and grade a subset, while others give a short list of problems at the end of Wednesday’s class. ... Toward the end of the term, the students handed only in the smaller subset of problems which would be graded since by this time they should have learned what was expected for a complete mathematical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a grading policy that balances workload and feedback: either collect all and grade samples or have students submit a designated subset; change submission patterns over the term to reflect learning progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage peer review but require independent final write-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Although I encouraged the students to discuss their graded solutions with other members of their group before working on resubmits, time pressure from other courses made this an unrealistic expectation. ... perhaps some peer review can be part of the grading scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote peer discussion and review as a learning tool and consider building structured peer review into grading, but require the final written solutions to be independent to ensure individual assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain cohort pacing in larger classes
rubrics_metrics.description: In larger classes (especially those with fluid group membership) it is important for most of the students to be at about the same place most of the time: at a minimum, they should finish the chapters at about the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assignments, pacing, and instructor interventions to keep the class moving roughly in sync, preventing fragmentation of understanding across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage larger class advantages (more approaches, wrap-up sharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are possible advantages to a larger class. For example, there were always students who were eager to report on their group’s work or to voice their group’s unresolved questions in an end-of-class wrap up. For harder problems, several different approaches would sometimes result in spirited arguments that continued after class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage end-of-class wrap-ups and sharing of diverse approaches; use class size to create more opportunity for varied strategies and extended discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of puzzle problems to build intuition for indirect reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the transition from elementary logic to proof, it can be helpful to assign puzzle problems, such as Raymond Smullyan’s knights and knaves. ... working on them helps develop a basis of intuition for proof by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce logic puzzles early to develop intuition for indirect reasoning and proof by contradiction; discuss solutions in class to illustrate inference rules and deductive flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach natural deduction with concrete tools (Tarski’s World)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accompanying courseware shows students how, among other things, to produce natural deduction proofs of statements about the shapes in the world. ... use of these materials improves students’ ability to reason deductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use software (e.g., Tarski’s World) or formal natural deduction exercises to train students in deductive proof construction; evidence suggests this transfers to improved reasoning in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin proof instruction with disproof by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: One can start by giving students statements to identify as true or false, asking them to justify a determination of true 'as best as you can' and to support an answer of false by providing a counterexample. ... most students find it easier to understand and construct disproofs by counterexample than to understand and construct even simple direct proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use true/false tasks emphasizing counterexamples to make explicit that one counterexample disproves a universal statement and to motivate the need for general proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach structure of direct proof: identify 'suppose' and 'to show'
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important initial point to communicate to beginning students about proving a universal statement is that they will have to move from something that is supposed to be true to something that must be shown. ... A direct proof of such a statement has the following outline: Suppose that x is a particular but arbitrarily chosen (or 'generic') element of the set for which the hypothesis is true. We must show that x also makes the conclusion true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly teach students to identify the hypothesis ('suppose') and the conclusion ('to show'), to choose a generic particular element, and to reason from definitions to derive the conclusion for that generic element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate proof by contraposition and contradiction by their 'suppose' and 'to show'
rubrics_metrics.description: In a direct proof one supposes one has a particular but arbitrarily chosen object that satisfies the hypothesis, and one shows that this object satisfies the conclusion. In a proof by contraposition one supposes one has a particular but arbitrarily chosen object for which the conclusion is false, and one shows that for this object the hypothesis is also false. In a proof by contradiction one supposes that the entire statement to be proved is false, and one shows that this supposition leads to a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to recognize the different starting assumptions and targets for the three proof methods and to choose the method appropriate to the problem structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions operationally and emphasize bidirectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: To answer the question 'How do I show that the conclusion follows from the hypothesis?' the prover needs an operational understanding of the 'if' direction of the definitions of the mathematical terms in the conclusion. ... Note that, although they are frequently stated less formally, definitions are actually bidirectional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students to translate formal definitions into operational 'if' and 'only if' forms so they can derive consequences and work forward/backward in proofs; stress extracting usable proof steps from definitions (e.g., 'n is even' means 'n = 2k for some integer k').

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure problem sequences as games to engage discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of writing the last sequence of problems as a game originated with the Fall 2003 Math 399 class ... A game evolved in which one group member would give a Prüfer code for their personal private tree and the rest of the group would then find the tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interactive, game-like problem sequences (e.g., produce codes and reconstruct objects) to deepen intuition and engagement while guiding students toward formal bijections and proofs.
